answer.rationale: The write-path degradation began ~90 minutes ago, closely following a release 2 hours prior, and is confined to the primary region while settlement writes are at peak—this pattern is most consistent with a bad build rather than pure load or a dependency failure. memory_b1 supports rollback as a fast, low-risk mitigation that historically cleared a similar error spike without customer impact, so I verify it to confirm the original record still shows clean completion and no write loss. I also verify memory_b2 (regional failover) because the region-confined symptom makes failover tempting, but failover during heavy write traffic risks losing in-flight settlement writes if replication isn't synchronous, which conflicts with the primary objective; checking the source record helps rule out or support that option before committing capacity elsewhere. Add_capacity, circuit_breaker, and read_replica routing address load, dependency, or read-path issues respectively, none of which clearly matches a write-path regression starting right after a deploy. Given only one intervention is possible, rollback is applied broadly (not a guarded test) since this is an active incident requiring full mitigation, but I flag that reverting the release also discards any legitimate changes it shipped, and the causal link between the release and the latency spike remains inferred rather than confirmed.
